title: Exodus 24:1–11
context: The covenant is ratified at Sinai. Moses tells the people all the LORD’s words, and they answer together that they will do them. Moses writes the words, builds an altar with twelve pillars, and has offerings made. He reads the book of the covenant, and after the people pledge obedience he sprinkles them with the blood of the covenant. Then Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders go up, see the God of Israel, and eat and drink in his presence unharmed.

verses.text: He said to Moses, “Come up to the LORD, you, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel; and worship from a distance.
verses.arminianNotes: God summons Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders to come up and worship from a distance. Arminian readers note the graded access: the whole people is represented, yet distance is kept before God’s holiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the ordered approach to God’s holiness: representatives, mediation, and distance. That structure points forward to the tabernacle and finally to Christ, through whom believers draw near, as Hebrews 10:19–22 says.

verses.text: Moses alone shall come near to the LORD, but they shall not come near. The people shall not go up with him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Moses alone may come near. Arminian readers see Moses’ unique role as mediator, appointed by God, standing between the holy God and the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress mediation as God’s appointed way of approach. Moses foreshadows Christ, the one mediator between God and humanity in 1 Timothy 2:5 and the mediator of a better covenant in Hebrews 8:6.

verses.text: Moses came and told the people all the LORD’s words, and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice, and said, “All the words which the LORD has spoken we will do.”
verses.arminianNotes: The people respond with one voice: All the words which the LORD has spoken we will do. Arminian readers see a genuine, voluntary covenant commitment, a free response to God’s gracious initiative in the exodus.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see a sincere pledge. They note that Israel’s later failures expose the limits of human resolve and point to the need for the new covenant in which God writes his law on the heart, as Jeremiah 31:31–34 says.
verses.keyContrast: Both see a real and freely spoken commitment that Israel soon breaks. Arminian readers typically emphasize the genuine human response in covenant-making. Reformed readers typically emphasize what the pledge reveals about human inability apart from new-covenant grace, though they too affirm the pledge was sincere.

verses.text: Moses wrote all the LORD’s words, then rose up early in the morning and built an altar at the base of the mountain, with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Moses writes all the LORD’s words and builds an altar with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes. Arminian readers note the importance of the written covenant, which every generation can read and answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inscripturation of God’s word as foundational: covenant and canon go together. The twelve pillars show that the whole people stands in the covenant before God.

verses.text: He sent young men of the children of Israel, who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of cattle to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Young men offer burnt offerings and peace offerings. Arminian readers see consecration and fellowship: burnt offerings express full devotion, and peace offerings express communion with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see sacrifice as the necessary ground of covenant fellowship. Before Aaronic priests were appointed, sacrifice already shows that sinners approach God through blood.

verses.text: Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar.
verses.arminianNotes: Half the blood is put in basins and half sprinkled on the altar. Arminian readers note that the ritual binds both parties: God’s side is signified by the altar and the people’s side by the blood still to be sprinkled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the two-part rite as uniting God and people in covenant through blood, with the altar representing God’s presence and acceptance.

verses.text: He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said, “We will do all that the LORD has said, and be obedient.”
verses.arminianNotes: Moses reads the book of the covenant, and the people pledge to do all and be obedient. Arminian readers stress that the people respond to a clearly heard word: informed, public consent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word preached before the covenant is sealed, which they relate to word and sacrament in Christian worship. The people’s vow echoes 24:3.

verses.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which the LORD has made with you concerning all these words.”
verses.arminianNotes: Moses sprinkles the people with the blood of the covenant. Jesus echoes these words at the Last Supper in Matthew 26:28, and Hebrews 9:18–20 cites this scene. Arminian readers see the old covenant inaugurated by blood, pointing to Christ’s blood shed for all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see Christ’s words fulfilling this scene: his blood inaugurates the new covenant. They commonly connect the covenant blood with its effective application to God’s covenant people.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm Christ’s blood of the covenant as the fulfillment of this rite. Arminian readers typically connect it with an atonement provided for all and received by faith. Reformed readers typically connect it with Christ’s definite work for his covenant people, though the tradition’s confessions also teach its infinite sufficiency.

verses.text: Then Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up.
verses.arminianNotes: Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders go up. Arminian readers note the solemn privilege of Israel’s leaders, and the sobering fact that Nadab and Abihu later die for unauthorized fire in Leviticus 10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that great privilege does not guarantee faithfulness, as Nadab and Abihu’s later judgment shows.

verses.text: They saw the God of Israel. Under his feet was like a paved work of sapphire stone, like the skies for clearness.
verses.arminianNotes: They saw the God of Israel. The text describes only what was under his feet, a pavement like sapphire, which WEB’s footnote says may be lapis lazuli, clear as the sky. Arminian readers note the restraint: they see a revelation of God, not his full being, in light of 33:20.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the same restraint. Many identify what they saw as a theophany, a visible manifestation, while God’s essence remains invisible, as John 1:18 and 1 Timothy 6:16 say. Ezekiel 1:26 uses similar imagery.

verses.text: He didn’t lay his hand on the nobles of the children of Israel. They saw God, and ate and drank.
verses.arminianNotes: God did not lay his hand on the nobles; they saw God and ate and drank. Arminian readers see grace: sinners in God’s presence are spared and welcomed to a covenant meal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a covenant meal of communion made possible by the blood just sprinkled. Many Christian readers see an anticipation of the Lord’s Supper and the marriage supper of the Lamb.
